opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think evals are one of the most underrated levers we have. People tend to think of them as purely measurement, something you run at the end to see how you did. But in practice, what you choose to measure ends up shaping what the whole organization optimizes for. Researchers naturally gravitate toward the numbers that are on the dashboard, so if you pick the wrong eval, you can spend months making real progress on something that doesn't actually matter.

So the first thing I think about is: does this eval actually capture the capability we care about, or is it a proxy that's going to get saturated or gamed? A lot of classic benchmarks were great for a while, but once models got good enough, the remaining errors were mostly label noise or ambiguity, and pushing on them stopped telling you anything useful.

The second thing is we try to build evals that sit a bit ahead of where the models are. If you want a model that can do long-horizon reasoning, or real software engineering, or genuine research-style problem solving, you need tasks where today's model mostly fails but where you can clearly verify success. That gap is what gives the team a target. Competition math and programming were really nice for this, because the answers are checkable and the difficulty scales almost indefinitely.

And then there's a kind of humility piece. You have to keep checking that gains on the eval correspond to gains people actually feel when they use the model. When those two things diverge, that's usually a sign the eval has drifted from what you meant it to measure, and it's time to retire it and build the next one.

r001.rationale: The response says an eval should capture the capability the team cares about and describes building tasks for specific desired capabilities, with success that can be clearly verified.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that evals are the thing that actually steers the research, more than people realize from the outside. Whatever you measure is what the org optimizes for, so choosing the eval is close to choosing the capability you'll end up with.

The way I think about it is: you start from the thing you actually care about, not the thing that's easy to measure. Early on with code, the easy thing was to grab a bunch of existing benchmarks that looked like programming. But what we really wanted to know was, can this model write a function from a natural language description that actually runs and passes tests? So we built HumanEval around that, with hidden unit tests, because that's the capability, not "does it autocomplete plausible-looking tokens." Once we had a measure that tracked the real thing, progress on it meant real progress.

The second piece is you want evals that have headroom and that are hard to game. A benchmark that's saturated tells you nothing, and a benchmark that leaks into pretraining data tells you something misleading, which is worse. So we spend a lot of time on contamination, on fresh problems, on things like competition math and competitive programming where there's a clean notion of correctness and a long ladder of difficulty. The ladder matters. You want to be able to see the model climbing from easy problems to problems that very few humans can do, because that gradient is what you're going to hill-climb on.

Third, you have to accept that every eval is a proxy and it will eventually break. Models get good at the proxy in ways that don't generalize. So you keep a portfolio: some narrow, crisp, automatically gradable things, and then some messier evals that are closer to real usage, including human preference and actually having people use the model for real tasks. When the crisp evals and the messy evals disagree, that's usually the most informative moment, because it tells you your proxy has drifted from the thing you wanted.

And then the last thing, which is maybe the most important: you have to decide what capabilities you want in the first place, and that's a values question as much as a research question. We care about reasoning, about reliability over long horizons, about the model knowing when it doesn't know. Those are harder to measure than accuracy on a multiple-choice set, but if you don't build evals for them, you simply won't get them. So a lot of the work is sitting down and asking, what would convince us the model is actually better in the way we care about, and then being willing to build that measurement even when it's expensive.

r001.rationale: The response says to start from the capability the team cares about, build an evaluation that measures it, and that capabilities without evaluations will not be developed. This communicates that desired capabilities need evaluations to assess whether they are achieved.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what do you actually want the model to be useful for? It’s easy to start with a benchmark because it’s available, and then gradually substitute doing well on that benchmark for the capability you cared about.

So I’d work backward from concrete tasks. If you want a model to help with research, can it formulate a useful hypothesis, design an experiment, and interpret a result? Those are different things, and a single score can hide where it’s struggling.

Then you need to keep checking whether improvements transfer. If the benchmark goes up, but people aren’t finding the model more useful on unfamiliar problems, that’s a signal to revisit the evaluation. The eval is a proxy for what you want, and you have to keep questioning that proxy.

r001.rationale: The response recommends working backward from concrete tasks and notes that a single score can hide weaknesses, but it does not clearly state that each desired capability needs its own evaluation measuring whether that capability was successfully elicited.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of evaluations as a way to make the goal concrete. If we say we want a model to be better at coding, what do we actually mean? Solving a short problem is one thing; working in a large repository, figuring out an ambiguous bug, and checking that the fix works is another. The evaluation needs to capture the behavior we actually care about.

But you have to be careful, because once you optimize against an evaluation, you can get better at the test without getting better at the underlying task. So I’d want multiple signals: held-out problems, realistic tasks, and feedback from people using the model. And I’d spend time looking at failures, not just the aggregate score. Often that’s what tells you whether you’re missing a capability or whether your evaluation is measuring the wrong thing.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations should capture the behavior people care about, but does not clearly state that each desired capability needs an evaluation measuring whether that capability was successfully elicited.
